stem: Silver, Ag, is a metal in the d-block of the Periodic Table.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Silver can form compounds containing either $\text{Ag}^+$ or $\text{Ag}^{2+}$ ions.

Explain why silver is a transition element.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Table 1.1 gives data relevant to the Born-Haber cycle for silver(I) fluoride, $\text{AgF}$.

Table 1.1

| standard energy change | value/$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| first ionisation energy of silver | +732 |
| enthalpy change of atomisation of silver | +289 |
| enthalpy change of atomisation of fluorine | +79 |
| enthalpy change of formation of silver(I) fluoride | -203 |
| lattice energy of silver(I) fluoride | -955 |

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
Write equations for the standard enthalpy changes described. Include state symbols.

- standard enthalpy change of atomisation of silver

- standard enthalpy change of formation of silver(I) fluoride

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text:
Calculate the first electron affinity, $\text{EA}_1$, of fluorine, using data from Table 1.1.

It may be helpful to draw a labelled energy cycle as part of the working for your answer.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text:
Use the data in Table 1.2 to calculate the enthalpy change of solution, $\Delta H_{\text{sol}}$, of $\text{AgF(s)}$.

Table 1.2

| energy change at 298 K | value/$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| lattice energy of $\text{AgF(s)}$ | -955 |
| enthalpy change of hydration of $\text{Ag}^+\text{(g)}$ | -464 |
| enthalpy change of hydration of $\text{F}^-\text{(g)}$ | -506 |

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Use your answer to (c)(i) to suggest whether AgF is soluble in water at 298 K. Explain your answer.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text:
Table 1.3 shows some data relevant to the silver(I) halides, $\text{AgCl}$ to $\text{AgI}$.

Table 1.3

| silver(I) halide | first electron affinity of halogen/$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | lattice energy /$\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $\text{AgCl}$ | -349 | -905 |
| $\text{AgBr}$ | -325 | -890 |
| $\text{AgI}$ | -295 | -876 |

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.text: Explain the trend in the first electron affinities of the halogens, $\text{Cl}$ to $\text{I}$.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: Explain the trend in the lattice energies of the silver(I) halides, $\text{AgCl}$ to $\text{AgI}$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text:
An electrochemical cell is constructed using the electrodes shown in Table 1.4.

Table 1.4

| electrode | half-equation | $E^{\ominus}/\text{V}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | $\text{AgCl(s)} + \text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag(s)} + \text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)}$ | +0.222 |
| 2 | $\text{Cu}^{2+}\text{(aq)} + 2\text{e}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Cu(s)}$ | +0.342 |

parts.label: (e)(i)
parts.text:
Calculate the standard cell potential, $E^{\ominus}_{\text{cell}}$.

Construct an equation for the overall cell reaction.

$E$

parts.label: (e)(ii)
parts.text:
In a different experiment, electrode 1 is set up using a saturated solution of $\text{KCl}$.

Saturated $\text{KCl(aq)}$ contains 36.0 g of $\text{KCl}$ per $100 \text{cm}^3$ of solution at 298 K.

The Nernst equation for electrode 1 is:

{{figure:pdf_visual_01.png}}

$$E = E^{\ominus} + \frac{0.059}{z} \log \frac{1}{[\text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)}]}$$

Calculate the electrode potential, $E$, of electrode 1 under these conditions.
